He describes the work as monotonous in a way that requires total attention, which is a combination that sounds contradictory until you watch the first twenty minutes.
The dwell time problem

Timetables allocate a dwell time at each station, typically well under a minute on a suburban service. That allocation assumes passengers board and alight in an orderly exchange. On a heavily loaded service the exchange is not orderly, and the doors, which on older rakes do not close at all, never define a clean boundary between boarding and departing.

The guard signals departure when the exchange is complete enough. That judgement is made in real time by a person watching a moving crowd, and it is the single most consequential discretionary decision in the operation of the network. Signal too early and someone is left hanging on; signal too late and the train behind is checked at the home signal.

Newer rakes with closing doors have changed this significantly on the sections where they run. Dwell becomes more predictable because the door close is a defined event rather than a judgement, and the safety improvement is obvious. The trade-off is that a door that will not close because of an obstruction produces a hard stop that an open-door rake never had.

With the old rakes you managed the crowd, with the new ones the crowd has to manage itself before the doors shut, said a guard with nineteen years on the same corridor, both are difficult, they are just difficult differently.
Running to a card

The motorman works to a running card listing every stop, the arrival and departure time at each, and the permanent speed restrictions on the section. Much of it is memorised after a few months on a link, but the card is consulted anyway, because a temporary speed restriction imposed for track work can appear on any day and is issued in the caution order at the start of the trip.

Braking on a suburban rake is a matter of timing rather than force. The train has to be brought to a stand with the driving cab at a marked point so that the rake sits correctly against the platform, and the deceleration has to be smooth enough that standing passengers, of whom there are hundreds, are not thrown. A hard stop generates complaints and, more importantly, injuries.

Signal sighting is continuous. Colour light signals on the suburban sections come up frequently at these headways, and the motorman calls them aloud, a practice that is both procedure and a way of keeping attention engaged through a shift that is mostly the same three minutes repeated forty times.
The things that go wrong

Overhead equipment failures, points that fail to set, a passenger on the track and, with grim regularity, a person struck while crossing. Each of these stops a section, and each requires a defined response that the crew executes before anyone senior has arrived. Motormen describe the first few minutes of an incident as entirely theirs, with control room support arriving after.

Monsoon is the seasonal transformation. Water on the track above a defined level halts services on the affected section entirely, because traction motors on a suburban rake sit low and flooding damages them. Every crew on a Mumbai suburban link has a story about a monsoon evening spent on a stalled rake with a thousand passengers and no way forward or back.

Crew management under disruption is a logistics problem in its own right. A motorman whose booked hours run out cannot simply continue, and relief has to reach a train that may be stopped between stations. Crew booking lobbies plan for this and are, by universal agreement among the crew, understaffed for the worst days.
What passengers do not see

Before the first trip the motorman signs on at the lobby, undergoes a breath analyser test, collects the caution order and the running card, and takes over the rake from the previous crew with a brake test and a walk-around. The handover is brief because the rake is turning around in the platform, and the walk-around is done at a pace that a safety auditor would call brisk.

Maintenance happens at night in the car sheds, where rakes are cleaned, examined and repaired in a window between the last service and the first. The shed staff work to a schedule as tight as the operating timetable and with the same absence of slack, and a rake that is not released on time removes a service from the morning peak.

At the end of the shift the motorman signs off, records any defects noted during the trips, and walks out through a station concourse that is still moving at the same density it was four hours ago. The card for tomorrow is already posted. The timetable will be the same, the crowd will be the same, and the ninety seconds at each platform will have to be found again.
